input: This summary brings together the background, the figures, and the thinking behind a proposed heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant, where refrigeration accounts for a substantial share of the site's electricity consumption. The plant in question uses 2552 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, so even a modest percentage improvement translates into a meaningful quantity of energy. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 11% of that use, which works out at a derived saving of 281 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Set against this, the capital cost is $426k, and at an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh the derived annual saving is $31k, giving a derived simple payback of 13.7 years. Viewed in the round, $426k is a considerable sum to commit against $31k a year, and the payback stretches well into the longer term. It is important to appreciate that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and that refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so there are genuine uncertainties wrapped around the headline numbers. Against that background, the recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision, so that measured performance can replace projection; the plant engineer owns the trial and will report what the metering shows. The metering exercise is deliberately modest in scope, since a single line can be instrumented without disturbing production on the rest of the site, and its results can be read directly against the projection.
target: The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision, and the plant engineer owns the trial. A food plant uses 2552 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 11% of that use, a derived saving of 281 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $426k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $31k and the derived simple payback is 13.7 years. The trade-off is $426k of capital committed now against a derived $31k per year, and it is unfavourable at the vendor figure without a measured saving behind it. A simple payback divides the capital by the annual saving and so takes no account of the timing of the savings, of maintenance, or of any change in the electricity price over the payback period. Those omissions are part of the figure's meaning and are carried with it wherever it is quoted. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The trial replaces the projection with a measurement on one line, taken under the plant's own load pattern, before capital is committed to the retrofit as a whole. Metering a single line bounds the cost of the check and leaves the other lines untouched until the measured figure is known. If the measured saving falls below the projection, the payback extends beyond the stated value and the case for extending the retrofit weakens accordingly. The decision the summary supports is the trial, not the retrofit.
